strings.name: Marina Silva
strings.role: Brazilian federal deputy and former environment minister
strings.summary: Marina Silva moved from an Amazonian rubber-tapping community into trade unionism and national politics. She represented Acre in the Senate and twice led environmental affairs under President Lula. Her work on forests and climate has also involved conflicts over environmental licensing, development policy and governing alliances. After leaving the ministry in 2026, she resumed her federal deputy duties and unsuccessfully contested a São Paulo Senate seat.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Recent activity is supported by a COP31 event record for 12 November and an interview on 14 November. Elections, service in office, resignation requests, formal departures and policy proposals are distinguished from one another and from measures already in force.
strings.influence.rationale: She entered national politics from Amazonian communities and has long promoted forest protection and environmental governance, becoming an important figure in global environmental policy.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 8 February 1958 in Rio Branco, Acre, Brazil. She grew up in a rubber-tapping community, moved to the city for literacy education as a teenager and graduated in history from the Federal University of Acre in 1984.
strings.facts.f2.label: Local and parliamentary service
strings.facts.f2.value: She served on Rio Branco’s city council in 1989–1991 and in Acre’s state assembly in 1991–1995 before representing Acre in the Senate. Her current federal deputy seat represents São Paulo for REDE, the Sustainability Network, in the 2023–2027 term.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Forest protection and international recognition
strings.highlights.h1.text: In the environment ministry, she promoted cooperation across government and linked forest protection with local livelihoods. UNEP awarded her its Champions of the Earth prize in 2007. Forest-governance results reflect the work of public institutions, local communities and others, rather than her individual efforts alone.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Proposals for climate-risk governance
strings.highlights.h2.text: In a November 2026 interview, she advocated a legal framework for climate emergencies, a scientific and technical committee and cooperation among federal, state and municipal authorities. She also discussed a just transition away from fossil fuels. These are policy positions, not evidence that a new office has been established or that she has been appointed to it.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Unsuccessful São Paulo Senate campaign
strings.timeline.t1.text: She placed fourth in the election for two Senate seats, receiving 7,862,400 votes, or 18.12% of valid candidate votes. The electoral court declared Guilherme Derrite and André do Prado elected; the result did not give her a new Senate term.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Leaves the ministry and resumes deputy duties
strings.timeline.t2.text: She left to contest elections in São Paulo. The formal decision appeared in that day’s extra edition of the federal official gazette, and João Paulo Capobianco succeeded her as minister. The Chamber recorded her return on the same day; reports on 31 March preceded the formal departure date.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Returns as environment minister
strings.timeline.t3.text: She was sworn in to lead environment and climate-change affairs as Lula returned to the presidency. Her federal deputy swearing-in was on 1 February, with leave for ministerial service from 3 February; the two offices have separate timelines.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Sustainability Network obtains registration
strings.timeline.t4.text: The Superior Electoral Court approved REDE’s registration by 7 votes to 0. Silva had helped initiate the party-building effort earlier. Its 2013 registration request was rejected for insufficient validated supporting signatures; formal approval came in 2015.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Socialist Party nominates her for president
strings.timeline.t5.text: After Eduardo Campos died in a plane crash, the Brazilian Socialist Party nominated his former vice-presidential running mate Silva to replace him, with Beto Albuquerque as her running mate. She had contested the 2010 presidential election for the Green Party. A party nomination did not confer the presidency.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Requests resignation as environment minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: She submitted her resignation to Lula and subsequently returned to the Senate amid disagreements over environmental policy and the government’s development agenda. The 13 May record concerns the request; it does not establish that every formal appointment procedure was completed that day.
strings.timeline.t7.title: First leads Brazil’s environment ministry
strings.timeline.t7.text: She became environment minister in Lula’s first administration, serving in this first stint until 2008. She took leave from the Senate to join the cabinet; ministerial service and the statutory term of a Senate seat are distinct.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Enters the federal Senate
strings.timeline.t8.text: Following her election in 1994, she began representing Acre and later won reelection. The Senate records terms of 1995–2003 and 2003–2011, including leave while serving as environment minister.
